_doc: The first-week question bank (preprocessor/onboarding.py). The morning briefing asks one a day in a chat mode; the reviewer mode answers them in one sitting (onboarding.py ask, scripts/install/user_init.py --phase preferences). An answer becomes a rule in ~/.ea/config/preferences.json: kind and scope come from the question, text is `topic: <the answer>`, quote is the answer, source is onboarding. Order is the order asked. No institution or personal names here: the user supplies those in the answers. A question with `privacy` records a keep rule (privacy_rules.py): the answer picks a level from `answers` (a number or the words), and the rule's text is that level's line in `rule_texts`. A question with `requires: local-model` is asked only where the user's own model is set up.

questions.question: Whose mail must never be buried, whatever else is going on?
questions.why: The briefing ranks these senders first and never folds them into a digest.
questions.example: My department chair, my program officers and my own students.

questions.question: Which newsletters or mailing lists should the EA skip entirely?
questions.why: A skipped list is archived in code and never reaches a briefing.
questions.example: The campus events digest and every vendor newsletter.

questions.question: What makes an item urgent enough to lead your briefing?
questions.why: The briefing uses its URGENT framing only for what you call urgent.
questions.example: A grant deadline inside 48 hours or a student in trouble; a reminder is never urgent.

questions.question: What should the EA never do on its own, even where the autonomy tiers allow it?
questions.why: This rule is checked before any do-and-tell action.
questions.example: Never archive mail from students; never fill a poll for me.

questions.question: Which days or blocks should stay free of meetings?
questions.why: A standing rule for the drafts and the briefing. The scheduler reads its rules only from the EA-Managed calendar, so to make a block hard, add an nm event there (docs/SETUP.md 'The EA-Managed calendar').
questions.example: Tuesday mornings are writing time; the first week of a semester is off limits.

questions.question: When should the EA not interrupt you at all?
questions.why: Proactive posts and alerts wait until the window ends.
questions.example: Nothing between 21:00 and 07:30, and nothing on Sundays.

questions.question: How do you sign off, and what tone do you want in drafts written as you?
questions.why: The writer follows this before any style it infers from sent mail.
questions.example: Sign with my first name; short and warm with students, formal with sponsors.

questions.question: Who should the EA never draft to without asking you first?
questions.why: A reply to such a person is surfaced as a question, never staged as a draft.
questions.example: My dean, anyone at a funding agency, and journalists.

questions.question: Which standing facts about your roles, grants or eligibility should the EA always know?
questions.why: A fact here corrects the briefing instead of being guessed again each day.
questions.example: I am not eligible for early-career awards; my lab is funded through 2028.

questions.question: Do you want a short briefing or a full one?
questions.why: Short keeps the do-list and one bookkeeping line; full keeps every section.
questions.example: Short on weekdays; full on Monday.

questions.question: Which funding opportunities are never worth showing you?
questions.why: The funding scan drops them before they reach a briefing or a digest.
questions.example: Standing BAAs, small internal seed grants and anything that needs industry match.

questions.question: How should the EA handle requests to review or edit?
questions.why: Review invitations are triaged on this rule before they reach you.
questions.example: Decline anything outside my field; accept at most one review a month.

questions.question: Once you have written back to a prospective student, how much of their mail may the assistant see?
questions.why: Their mail stays on your machine until you write back, and their files always do. Answer 1 to keep it all there, 2 for facts only (who wrote, when, and the times they offered or took), or 3 for a short summary made on your machine, the default. With 3 the assistant can remind you of a reply you owe and set up the meeting you offered.
questions.example: 3. A summary is fine once I have answered them.

rule_texts.local: Mail from prospective students stays on your machine, also after you write back.
rule_texts.facts: Once you have written to an applicant, the assistant sees only who wrote, when, and the times they offered or took.
rule_texts.summary: Once you have written to an applicant, the assistant may read a short summary of their mail, made on your machine. It never reads the mail itself.
